content: The development of a unique identifier (UID) system in health care progresses through various stages, each with distinct costs, benefits, and risks. Initially, name-based paper records are replaced with records labeled by a unique alphanumeric code for each individual, ensuring no personally identifiable information is included. This transition requires secure databases at health facilities. As the system matures, it expands to capture and link individuals’ interactions with the health care system across services, facilities, and time. The information technology (IT) infrastructure, including hardware and software, is critical for evolving toward a person-centered electronic health record system. Decisions must be made about repurposing existing IT elements and investing in new ones to fully develop the UID and electronic health record system. The starting point for implementation depends on the scope of data to be collected, the adaptability of current systems (including legacy systems), and the extent of system interoperability. Transitioning begins with creating a secure, interoperable database structure for health records, which can be accessed online or offline within and across facilities. Historically, health information systems, particularly for HIV case management, were developed in isolation, leading to fragmented systems with limited interoperability. Proprietary systems and insufficient capacity to maintain interoperability have exacerbated this issue. In contrast, advanced electronic record systems achieve full interoperability, linking data from various sources, including vital statistics, to track individuals lost to follow-up. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides resources to guide investment in digital health interventions and strengthen health systems, such as the Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG) and the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit. Introducing a UID system is a foundational step in building a person-centered health system, enabling individuals to access a range of services across facilities and over time. A UID system facilitates interoperability by providing an anonymous identifier that can be shared across devices, facilities, and disease programs to link data on the same individual. Privacy, security, and confidentiality are paramount in health care information systems. Risks are minimized by labeling records with content-free UIDs that do not include personal information, separating personal details from clinical records. Advanced stages of UID implementation involve categorizing health data by sensitivity and implementing differentiated access and security protocols to protect identifying elements like names and addresses. A fully developed national system requires legal, regulatory, and policy frameworks to protect data, along with enforcement mechanisms to address breaches promptly. Digitizing health care records enhances data analysis for program management, improvement, and research. In the early stages, data officers can upload information from paper records into electronic systems, enabling regular data quality assessments and the generation of management dashboards. As capacity builds, central analysis teams manage databases, conduct data quality assessments, and follow up on findings. Advanced systems support local analyses of care and program capacity using standardized dashboards, data visualization, and reports, ensuring data is regularly used for decision-making and management at all levels. The feasibility of UID implementation depends on national electricity and telecommunications infrastructure. Solutions may require a mix of online and offline systems, with advanced stages involving fully connected systems across facilities and community care. Cloud-based servers or regional servers can prevent single points of failure, offering accessible, flexible, and stable hosting infrastructure with robust security and data protection. Effective national health information systems must enable data sharing and understanding across clinics, hospitals, laboratories, pharmacies, and individuals, regardless of the application or vendor. To maximize the benefits of a UID system, it must include content-free alphanumeric identifiers, differentiated security for various data types, cross-references to local identifiers, encryption mechanisms, and administrative infrastructure. South Africa’s Health Patient Registration System (HPRS) exemplifies the implementation of a UID system. The HPRS assigns a health UID, the Health Patient Registration Number (HPRN), to individuals, enabling longitudinal tracking across facilities. This system improves service delivery and provides better data for strategic decision-making and planning. By 2019, the HPRS had registered over 45 million individuals, covering approximately 70% of the population. In Pakistan, the Nai Zindagi Trust uses UIDs to support people who inject drugs with HIV prevention and treatment services. Despite legal and social barriers, the organization provides services to approximately 34,000 individuals through mobile outreach at 44 sites across 58 districts. An electronic health management information system captures data at each service delivery point, linking service delivery components and inventory management. This system enables real-time updates, continuity of care, and safeguards against data breaches. Reports generated from the system monitor service delivery trends and outcomes, informing planning, resource allocation, and program improvement. Health care data, by nature, includes highly personal information. For marginalized populations, breaches of confidentiality can lead to stigma, discrimination, or even criminal arrest, discouraging interaction with the health care system. Privacy, security, and confidentiality are therefore critical. Transparent legislation ensuring rights-based access and control over personal health data empowers patients to participate in improving their health outcomes. Digital health systems must be designed and implemented with privacy, security, and confidentiality in mind to reduce risks and build trust, particularly among vulnerable populations.
